summary: Argues for standard host names for Telnet and recommends four-character names, with eight-character alternatives, for the hosts then on the network. Each host was expected to suggest its own call letters. Names would be case-insensitive.

eli5.summary: A shorter nickname list for the network's computers: four letters each, like call signs on a radio, with a longer version too.

subtitle: Four-letter nicknames for early ARPANET computers

tldr.problem: Early ARPANET hosts each had different names or call letters in use, making it hard for Telnet users to remember which host was which.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes standard four-character call letters for each host on the network, with optional eight-character variants, letting each host suggest its own mnemonic.
tldr.outcome: The proposal influenced how network hosts were named, though practice evolved differently over the years as the network grew and domain names later replaced numeric host tables.

today: RFC 233 is an informational document and has not been obsoleted. The naming scheme proposed here was one of several early approaches; later, the domain name system (DNS) replaced host tables and numeric addresses for everyday use on the internet.

sections.title: The Need for Standard Host Names
sections.content:
The ARPANET of 1971 had multiple computers at different sites. Telnet users had to know which host to connect to, but there was no standard way to refer to them. Different programs and different sites used different names or numbers. This RFC proposes standardizing on call letters using four characters, with eight-character names as alternatives.

The authors note that brevity and memorability are both valuable: a short code is easy to type, but a longer mnemonic is easier to remember. Their proposal balances both by offering both lengths.
sections.eli5: Each computer needs a short name people can type and remember, like how radio stations have call signs.

sections.title: The Proposed Naming Scheme
sections.content:
Each host number gets two names: a four-character short form and an eight-character long form. Upper and lower case are treated as equivalent, so typing is flexible. The RFC publishes a table of about 40 hosts with their proposed names, such as SEX for host 1 (UCLA), NIC for host 2 (SRI), and UTAH for host 4.

The authors recommend that each host organization should propose its own preferred call letters rather than having them imposed. This lets sites choose names that make sense in their own context.
sections.eli5: Each computer gets a short four-letter name and a longer eight-letter option, and the people running each computer can choose what they want to be called.

sections.title: Implementation and Adoption
sections.content:
The RFC notes that Telnet programs would use these call letters to let users type a simple name instead of a numeric address. Case-insensitive matching means a user could type sex, SEX, or Sex and reach the same host.

The proposal is straightforward: maintain a shared list of call letters, ensure all Telnet implementations recognize them, and let network sites update the list as new hosts join the network.
sections.eli5: Once everyone agrees on the names, Telnet programs can look them up so a user just types the name instead of a number.

references.text: Karp, P., "Proposed host-host protocol", RFC 226, September 1971.
